summary: Redwood AE/SE walked NovusAI through a migration-focused demo mapping OpenAI/Anthropic/Together API patterns to Redwood's API and Console. Discussion covered parity for chat, completions, embeddings, function calling, streaming, tokenization differences, batching for cost, Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC/private deployment considerations, KMS/keys, SOC 2 and audit logs. Agreed to run a short pilot; next steps include parity spreadsheet, benchmark scripts, and pilot kickoff.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (NovusAI CTO), Sara Kim (NovusAI ML Eng), Ethan Li (NovusAI Eng Mgr)

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll take about 45 minutes for the demo and save time for q's, uh Liam's gonna run the deep technical bits
[00:10] Rajiv Menon: Sounds good, thanks Maya, appreciate it
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: hi all, quick agenda, 1) parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API, 2) Console walkthrough, Optimize recommendations for batching/quant, 3) security and deployment options, and 4) pilot next steps
[00:35] Sara Kim: yeah we mainly care about function calling parity and streaming behavior -- also embeddings shape because our vector DB ingestion pipeline expects a certain format
[00:45] Liam O'Connor: totally. starting with chat / completions: on Redwood we have a unified /v1/generate and also a chat style endpoint. the mapping is straightforward -- role tokens are same idea but note Redwood includes a per-token cost model and optional system role enforcement. in practice your existing OpenAI chat calls map to Redwood chat with minimal changes -- prompt schema stays the same
[01:15] Ethan Li: what about function calling? we rely heavily on model-driven function calls for entity extraction
[01:22] Liam O'Connor: good question. Redwood supports function/tool calling -- semantics are similar to OpenAI with a few differences: the tool schema is accepted as JSON in the call, callbacks are sent as structured events. there was a small quirk in our older SDK where the name field sometimes got lowercased in the transcript, so watch for that -- sorry that's just a transcribe note
[01:45] Rajiv Menon: and Together models -- we use 'together-xyz' for some internal evals, any gotchas?
[01:51] Maya Patel: models are surfaced in our catalog, and for Together/Anthropic we map model families -- though tokenization might differ slightly. Liam can show the tokenizer diff and how we normalize token counts for cost parity
[02:05] [02:05] Liam O'Connor: (screen share) here's a parity sheet -- left column OpenAI/Anthropic/Together request, right column Redwood example. e.g., OpenAI chat.post with messages -> Redwood chat.messages array, function_call: 'auto' -> Redwood function_mode: 'auto'. embeddings: openai embeddings.create -> Redwood embeddings.batch with same dims returned. note: Together may include special eos tokens; our SDK strips and normalizes by default
[03:10] Sara Kim: when you say embeddings.batch, do we get the same vector dims? our downstream expects 1536 dims for the base model
[03:18] Liam O'Connor: yes, when you pick the equivalent model in Redwood, dims are preserved. we'll include exact model mapping in the spreadsheet. also supports batched inputs up to N entries per call -- default 64 but configurable
[03:35] Ethan Li: latency and cost, we've seen big differences between providers. how do you recommend balancing latency vs cost?
[03:42] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Optimize gives recommendations -- for low latency you can pin a dedicated pool, we do autoscale. for cost you can enable batching + prefix KV cache for repeated queries. example: QPS spike patterns -- with caching you save 20-40% token cost on typical chat flows. we'll show concrete numbers in the bench run
[04:10] [04:10] Rajiv Menon: Is the streaming response behavior identical? we stream to product UI so chunking matters
[04:18] Liam O'Connor: streaming is SSE-based or websockets; chunk semantics are similar but chunk sizes may differ because our runtime optimizes by token groups. keep an eye on stop sequences -- there's a small timing delta sometimes which can cause one extra token if you rely on very strict stop boundaries. we have fallback config to reduce extra tokens for SLO-sensitive apps
[04:45] Sara Kim: what about rate limiting and quotas? we have bursts sometimes from CICD tests
[04:51] Maya Patel: hosted API has per-key quotas and rate limits, Dedicated gives predictable throughput with SLA-backed targets and burst windows. for large CICD bursts you can request a temporary quota increase or route those requests to a non-prod Dedicated pool
[05:10] [05:10] Liam O'Connor: switching to the Console -- (screen) here's per-route latency breakdown, token cost by user, and the rollouts page. when you migrate you can create a route that mirrors your OpenAI usage patterns and then do canary traffic -- we support percentage-based rollouts and automatic fallbacks to another model family if latency QoS fails
[06:00] Ethan Li: do you have pre-built overlays for SSO/SAML and RBAC? security is a big blocker for us
[06:07] Maya Patel: yes, enterprise plans include SSO with SAML, SCIM provisioning, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs. for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management. we ship SOC 2 Type II artifacts and can do an on-site security review if needed
[06:30] Rajiv Menon: about VPC/private -- we have HIPAA-ish constraints; can we run on-prem or in VPC with logging kept internally?
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem appliance. control plane can be customer-managed and logs/audit are stored in your environment -- we also provide log-forwarder connectors for SIEMs like Splunk
[06:50] Sara Kim: tokenization differences -- you mentioned earlier normalization
[06:57] Liam O'Connor: right, e.g., Anthropic sometimes counts assistant prefix differently. we do a pre-tokenization step in the SDK so billing/token estimate aligns with what your app expects. we'll include a small script to show token counts across models in the parity sheet
[07:20] [07:20] Rajiv Menon: any pitfalls in prompt engineering when migrating?
[07:25] Liam O'Connor: mostly stop token and system instruction handling. some models respond better to explicit system prompts; we surface recommended prompt templates per model in Console. also function arg typing -- if you rely on implicit behavior you should test the returned JSON shapes during pilot
[07:50] Maya Patel: quick demo of a migration example -- we'll convert an OpenAI chat.request to Redwood. (reads) openai: chat.completions.create with messages and functions; redwood: /v1/chat with messages, function_mode: 'auto', tools: [schema]. Here's a live curl example -- same payload, small header change: Authorization: Bearer REDWOOD_KEY vs OPENAI_KEY
[08:40] [08:40] (audio clip muffled for a few secs)
[09:05] Ethan Li: how about SDKs? we use python and node heavily
[09:10] Liam O'Connor: we have first-class SDKs for python/node/go with near-identical call patterns. code change is usually 10-20 lines: init client, replace client chat call with Redwood.chat.create and adjust function param names. we will include before/after snippets in the parity doc
[09:40] Sara Kim: embedding batch ingestion -- do you provide async ingestion or is it client-side batching?
[09:46] Liam O'Connor: client-side batching is recommended; our SDK provides helpers for chunking and retries. for high throughput we support streaming ingest where embeddings are piped into the vector DB connector. also network egress costs are configurable in Dedicated/private setups
[10:10] [10:10] Rajiv Menon: curious about cost model specifics -- per-token vs per-inference?
[10:16] Maya Patel: hosted is per-token (generation & prompt) and per-embedding unit. Dedicated is capacity-based (monthly commit) which is better for predictable high-volume workloads. Optimize can recommend quantization profiles to reduce GPU cost while maintaining quality
[10:40] Liam O'Connor: on the topic of quantization -- we ship curated quant profiles and recommend them by workload; e.g., classification/text-generation vs instruction-tuning like chat. we can run a quick quality-vs-cost sweep during pilot
[11:05] [11:05] Sara Kim: any visible regressions when moving from Anthropic to Redwood-verified models? we care about hallucination rates
[11:12] Liam O'Connor: we run evaluation harnesses per model, tie regressions to prompt sets, and have rollback/rollout features. for mitigations, you can enable stricter sampling, lower temperature, or use model-chaining where a verifier model checks outputs
[11:40] Maya Patel: Security checklist -- KMS for keys, SSO/SAML, audit logs, SOC 2, encryption at rest and in transit. Liam, any note on HSM integrations?
[11:50] Liam O'Connor: yes we integrate with customer KMS and HSM for private deployments; keys never leave customer boundary in Private mode. for Hosted we offer BYOK with envelope encryption into our HSMs
[12:05] [12:05] Rajiv Menon: can you provide the SOC 2 pack and a penetration test report?
[12:11] Maya Patel: yes we will share SOC 2 Type II and summary pentest report -- we'll send the secure link via our portal
[12:25] Ethan Li: network egress / data residency -- we need EU residency for certain data sets
[12:30] Liam O'Connor: we have region controls and can provision Dedicated/Private in EU regions; data residency is configurable and we can include that in the SLA addendum
[12:50] [12:50] Sara Kim: for pilot, can we start with a small model mapping and then scale?
[12:56] Maya Patel: recommended approach: 1) parity script and unit tests, 2) small pilot (1k-10k queries/day) to validate correctness, 3) perf run to measure latency/cost, 4) production migration with canary rollout
[13:20] (demo continues, screen shows Console routing config)
[15:00] [15:00] Liam O'Connor: tradeoffs: Dedicated gives predictability and lower unit cost but requires commit; Hosted quicker to start. Private gives maximum security but longer lead time. We'll tailor pilot to your constraints
[15:35] Rajiv Menon: for the pilot metrics we care about latency p50/p95, token cost delta, and accuracy/hallucination on our eval set
[15:44] Liam O'Connor: noted -- we'll include those as targets in the pilot runbook
[16:05] [16:05] Sara Kim: can you outline the minimal changes to our ingestion pipeline?
[16:10] Liam O'Connor: minimal: swap API base URL and auth header, adjust embed.batch call shape if you batch differently, and add our token estimator helper. we'll give a migration checklist in the doc
[16:30] (brief back and forth on rates, SDK version mismatches, a minor audio quirk captured as 'nh-uh')
[18:00] [18:00] Maya Patel: let's recap and confirm next steps. action items: maya to send parity mapping, liam to send bench scripts, rajiv share dataset, schedule pilot kickoff. any other questions?
[18:15] Rajiv Menon: no, that's great. thanks for the clear examples -- helps align internal eng and data teams
[18:22] Ethan Li: can we get a cost estimate for a 100k queries/month baseline?
[18:27] Maya Patel: yes, we'll include a hosted per-token estimate and a Dedicated sizing example in the spreadsheet
[18:35] Sara Kim: please include example curl and node/python SDK snippets -- fewer surprises for our platform team
[18:40] Maya Patel: will do. we'll also attach SOC2/security pack link and a small FAQ about function calling differences
[18:50] Rajiv Menon: perfect, thanks all
[18:55] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials, and liam will be on the pilot setup. end call
